fieldworkDocument.title: Measgaichte / Miscellaneous
fieldworkDocument.note: [NOTES: some notes in pencil most probably added by K. D. MacDonald. See below for details.]

item.description: a wife or female partner suspecting her partner of seeing another woman behind her back. [NOTES: note added in pencil: ’g eudach.]
used when someone is in good fettle. “Bha sogan math air an diugh.”
to gather, e.g. a dog gathering sheep or hens.
a wick in a lamp. Also heard as ‘sinneag’.
a nuisance or pest. “Tha miothlaint a’ tighinn thugainn an diugh.”
Do dhosan – your fringe or forelock. Think this is a Lewis word in origin for most people in Southern Isles use ‘logaidh’ for fringe or forelock.
being restricted or limited to do anything due to an irritating pain for example. “Chan urrainn dhomh sin a dheanamh an diugh oir tha mi uireasach le’m chois.”
a term used in childbirth to mean that the woman is near delivery.
used to mean labour pains. “Bha i pulla mór ann an saothair.”
a haymaking term meaning that the hay is in between being wet and dry, but not dry enough to be made into ricks. “O chan eil e ach plamaranda gu leòr an diugh fhathast.”
not caring, not bothered. “O chan eil iad sin ag abhsadh dè a thachras co-dhiu.”

means a long drawn out walk. As in the saying: “Rinneachadh bò chaol a’ tighinn gu baile feasgar fann foghair, rinneachadh bò chaol a’ tighinn gu baile.” Implies casualness, paying no attention to time, etc. [NOTES: note added in pencil: ?righinneachadh.]
a brief shower of rain lasting for a few minutes only.
mumbling kind of conversation which is difficult to understand.
an expression which would be used of a regular visitor. “Bhiodh e an taigh Sheonaidh air an oirlich [sic].”
